facts.statehood_note: One of the original 13 states; this is the date Delaware ratified the U.S. Constitution, the first state to do so, which is why it is called the First State.
facts.nickname: The First State (official since 2002, after a request from a first-grade class); also the Diamond State and the Blue Hen State
borders: New Jersey (across the Delaware River and Delaware Bay)

symbols.name: Blue Hen chicken (1939), linked to Delaware soldiers in the Revolutionary War
Peach blossom (1895), from the days when Delaware orchards had more than 800,000 peach trees
Ladybug (1974), after a campaign by second graders in Milford

facts.name_origin: Named for Delaware Bay, which was named after Thomas West, Lord De La Warr, an English nobleman and the first colonial governor of Virginia.

government.chambers: Delaware Senate (21 members, 4-year terms) and Delaware House of Representatives (41 members, 2-year terms); it meets at Legislative Hall in Dover.
government.executive: Governor (4-year term; cannot be elected a third time). The constitution gives the governor "the supreme executive powers of this State."
government.courts: Delaware Supreme Court (5 justices: a chief justice and four associate justices, appointed by the governor and confirmed by the Senate for 12-year terms). Delaware also has a Court of Chancery, a Superior Court and a Family Court.
government.local: Only 3 counties, the fewest of any state: New Castle (north), Kent (center) and Sussex (south). Counties were once split into areas called hundreds, which are now used only in land records.
government.constitution: Delaware's fourth and current constitution was adopted in convention on June 4, 1897. Earlier constitutions came in 1776, 1792 and 1831, and the Delaware Declaration of Rights was adopted on September 11, 1776.
government.kid_line: "The free communication of thoughts and opinions is one of the invaluable rights of humanity." (Delaware Constitution, Article I, Section 5)

long_ago.nation: The Lenape (Lenni Lenape, also called the Delaware)
long_ago.about: Unami-speaking Lenape lived mostly along the coast and the Delaware River, in a homeland they call Lenapehoking that also took in parts of New Jersey, Pennsylvania and New York. They hunted and farmed, and later traded furs with Europeans.

The Nanticoke, an Algonquian-speaking people of the Chesapeake Bay area, lived across much of the southern Delmarva Peninsula. They met English captain John Smith in 1608 and traded beaver pelts with the English.
The Susquehannock traded furs with the Lenape, who were their old rivals. They were defeated by the Haudenosaunee (Five Nations) in the 1670s.

today.nation: Nanticoke Indian Tribe (Nanticoke Indian Association), Millsboro
today.about: State recognized since 1922; the association was legally recognized in 1881 and runs a museum and community programs.

today.nation: Lenape Indian Tribe of Delaware, Cheswold
today.about: State recognized since August 3, 2016; it is not federally recognized, and the federally recognized Delaware Nation does not accept it as a Lenape nation.

first_peoples.today_note: Delaware has no federally recognized tribes. Most Lenape people were forced west, and the federally recognized Lenape nations today are the Delaware Nation and the Delaware Tribe of Indians, both in Oklahoma, and the Stockbridge-Munsee Community in Wisconsin. Some Nanticoke descendants live among the Delaware Tribe in Oklahoma and at Six Nations of the Grand River in Ontario, Canada.
sites: Nanticoke Indian Museum, Millsboro (run by the Nanticoke Indian Association)

history.event: The Lenape live along the Delaware River and coast, and the Nanticoke live in the southern part of the Delmarva Peninsula.
English captain John Smith meets the Nanticoke, who begin trading beaver pelts with the English.
The Dutch build a trading post called Zwaanendael near present-day Lewes. Within a year the settlers are killed in a dispute with Indigenous people living there.

Peter Minuit leads Swedes, Finns and Dutch to build Fort Christina (now in Wilmington), the start of New Sweden on Lenape land. The Dutch take over New Sweden in 1655, and the English take over in 1664.
William Penn takes control of the "Lower Counties on the Delaware." In 1704 the three counties begin meeting in their own assembly at New Castle.
On June 15, Delaware declares itself free of British and Pennsylvania rule. The same year, Delaware bans bringing in enslaved people from outside, but slavery stays legal.
On December 7, Delaware becomes the first state to ratify the U.S. Constitution.
Peter Spencer, who had been enslaved, starts the Union Church of Africans in Wilmington, a church run by Black Americans, and begins the Big August Quarterly gathering, which still meets today.

Wilmington is a key stop on the Underground Railroad. Thomas Garrett helps freedom seekers, including people guided by Harriet Tubman, and Samuel D. Burris is arrested in 1847 for guiding freedom seekers.
Delaware is still a state where slavery is legal, but 91.7% of its Black residents are free: about 19,829 free Black people and 1,798 enslaved people.
On January 3, Delaware's lawmakers vote against secession, and Delaware stays in the Union during the Civil War. Most Delawareans who fought served in the Union army.
In February the legislature votes against the 13th Amendment. Slavery in Delaware ends only when the 13th Amendment is ratified nationwide in December 1865.

During Reconstruction, Delaware lawmakers treat Black citizens as second-class, limit their voting rights despite the 15th Amendment, and pass segregation laws. Delaware does not ratify the 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments until 1901.

trailblazers.name: Absalom Jones
trailblazers.text: Born enslaved in Sussex County, he raised money through donations and loans to buy his wife's freedom so their children would be born free, and he won his own freedom in 1784. In Philadelphia he and Richard Allen founded the Free African Society in 1787. In 1802 he became the first African American ordained as a priest in the Episcopal Church.

trailblazers.name: Thomas Garrett
trailblazers.text: A Wilmington hardware merchant, he openly helped more than 2,500 people escape slavery and was a friend and helper to Harriet Tubman, giving her money and shoes. In 1848 a court found him guilty of helping a family of seven escape and gave him a heavy fine, but he kept helping freedom seekers.

trailblazers.name: Samuel D. Burris
trailblazers.group: Free Black American Underground Railroad conductor
trailblazers.text: Born free in Willow Grove, Kent County, he guided freedom seekers north to Pennsylvania. Arrested in 1847, he was put on the auction block to be sold into slavery, but abolitionist Isaac Flint secretly bought him and set him free.

trailblazers.name: Mary Ann Shadd Cary
trailblazers.group: Black American woman, journalist and teacher
trailblazers.text: Born in Wilmington to free Black parents whose home sheltered freedom seekers, she opened a school for Black children at 16. In 1853 she founded the Provincial Freeman newspaper, becoming the first Black woman publisher in North America. Later she studied law.

trailblazers.name: Annie Jump Cannon
trailblazers.text: Born in Dover, she learned the constellations from her mother. At Harvard she helped create the system astronomers use to sort stars by temperature, and by 1913 she could classify about 200 stars an hour. She lost most of her hearing as a young adult and was also a suffragist.

trailblazers.name: Louis L. Redding
trailblazers.group: Black American lawyer and civil rights leader
trailblazers.text: In 1929 he became the first African American lawyer in Delaware. In 1950 he won a case that made the University of Delaware admit Black students, and his 1952 cases against school segregation in Claymont and Hockessin became part of Brown v. Board of Education.

landforms: Atlantic Coastal Plain (flat, sandy and in places swampy)
Piedmont Plateau hills in the far north
Delmarva Peninsula (Delaware covers its northeast part)
Ebright Azimuth, the highest point (about 448 feet)
Lowest average elevation of any state
geography.regions: The northern tip of Delaware is the hilly Piedmont; south of a line between Newark and Wilmington, the rest of the state is the flat Atlantic Coastal Plain, with a low ridge in the west that sends water east to Delaware Bay or west to the Chesapeake Bay.

ecosystems.name: Delaware Bay beaches
ecosystems.about: Each spring hundreds of thousands of horseshoe crabs come ashore to lay eggs, with the peak in May. Shorebirds like the threatened red knot stop on their way to the Arctic and eat so many crab eggs that they double their weight in about two weeks.

ecosystems.name: Tidal salt marsh
ecosystems.about: Bombay Hook National Wildlife Refuge protects one of the largest tidal salt marshes left in the mid-Atlantic. It is a resting and breeding place for migrating birds.

ecosystems.name: Bald cypress swamp
ecosystems.about: The Great Cypress Swamp in southern Delaware and Maryland is one of the northernmost bald cypress swamps, a kind of swamp common farther south, and the largest unbroken forest on the Delmarva Peninsula.

ecosystems.name: Coastal and oak forests
ecosystems.about: Northern Delaware has mixed oak forests, and the south has Middle Atlantic coastal forests where American holly, the state tree, can grow 60 feet tall.

science.weather: Delaware has long, hot, humid summers with short, strong afternoon thunderstorms. Winters are cool to cold in the north and milder by the ocean: Wilmington averages about 20 inches of snow and Lewes about 10. Because the land is so low, coastal storms can push the sea inland; a severe storm in 1878 destroyed beach resorts and broke through the dunes at Bombay Hook.
science.resources: Farms raise broiler chickens, soybeans, corn and milk, and fishers catch crabs and clams. Delaware also makes chemicals and other products; the DuPont chemical company grew up here, and many big U.S. companies are legally based in Delaware.
science.highlight: Horseshoe crabs! Delaware Bay has more horseshoe crabs than any other place in the world. They are a key food for more than a million shorebirds, and a substance in their blue blood is used to test medicines and vaccines for germs.

g3_ss.title: Delaware's Communities and Government
g3_ss.plan: Find Dover, learn what the governor and General Assembly do, map the three counties, and read Article I, Section 5 of Delaware's constitution.

g3_ss.title: Delaware's First Peoples
g3_ss.plan: Meet the Lenape and Nanticoke of long ago, and learn where Lenape and Nanticoke people live today.

g3_ss.title: Delaware Trailblazers
g3_ss.plan: Meet Absalom Jones, Mary Ann Shadd Cary, Annie Jump Cannon and Louis Redding, and ask what new path each one opened.

g45_ss.title: Delaware's First Nations
g45_ss.plan: Compare Lenape and Nanticoke ways of life and the fur trade, and trace how land loss pushed many Lenape and Nanticoke people west and north.

g45_ss.title: Dutch, Swedish and English Delaware
g45_ss.plan: Trace Zwaanendael, New Sweden, Dutch and English rule, William Penn's Lower Counties, the 1776 break and ratification on December 7, 1787.

g45_ss.title: Delaware 1787–1877: A Border State
g45_ss.plan: Investigate how a slave state that stayed in the Union had mostly free Black residents, the Underground Railroad (Garrett, Burris, Tubman), Peter Spencer's church, and Delaware's fight against Black rights during Reconstruction.

g3_sci.title: Horseshoe Crabs and Shorebirds
g3_sci.plan: Follow horseshoe crabs to Delaware Bay beaches each May and learn how red knots depend on their eggs.

g3_sci.title: Marsh, Swamp and Forest
g3_sci.plan: Compare a tidal salt marsh, a bald cypress swamp and a holly forest, and what lives in each.

g3_sci.title: Living on Low Land
g3_sci.plan: Learn why Delaware is so flat and low, measure rain and tides, and find out how storms and high water change the coast.

g45_sci.title: Delaware Bay Food Web
g45_sci.plan: Build a food web around horseshoe crab eggs and use red knot weight data to explain why timing matters.

g45_sci.title: Coastal Plain and Piedmont
g45_sci.plan: Use maps and rock samples to compare Delaware's Piedmont and Coastal Plain, and explain the fall line between Newark and Wilmington.

g45_sci.title: Wetlands, Storms and Sea Level
g45_sci.plan: Use Bombay Hook's history and tide data to explain how marshes protect the coast and how storms reshape it.
